newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia jobs market still seen subdued.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia jobs market still seen subdued.

text.p: Australian employment is expected to remain subdued in coming months but there are some signs that the sector can be expected to turn up by the middle of next year, economists said on Thursday.
Coming just one day after the Reserve Bank of Australia's decision to lower the official cash rate to 6.0 percent from 6.5 percent, the data had little market impact.
Employment rose strongly for the second successive month in November, with the 24,400 rise almost matching October's 25,500 increase, offical figures showed.
The unemployment rate fell to 8.5 percent, its lowest level since July, from 8.8 percent in October.
Both the employment rise and unemployment rate came in on the strong side of expectations, which had centred on a 10,000 employment rise and an 8.5 percent unemployment rate.

While that strength in the last two months has seen employment levels rise by almost 50,000, over the first 11 months of the year it is up just 61,600 and the outlook is for subdued growth in coming months, economists said.

"Jobs growth of this magnitude, but driven by more full-time employment, will have to continue for several months before it can be said with any conclusiveness that the labour market is picking up," Societe Generale economist Glenn Maguire said.
Of the total rise, full time employment accounted for only 5,600 positions, and over the first 11 months of the year, full time employment has only risen by 21,900 positions.
Economists see full time employment growth as a sign of labour market strength because if companies are taking on full time workers it points to business confidence in the economy.
As full time wages are generally higher than those paid to part-time workers, full time jobs growth is also seen generating greating spending power which should further boost activity.

Westpac senior economist John Peters said that as most of the growth in November employment, and in employment in 1996, had been in part time jobs, "it doesn't really alter our view that labour market conditions are pretty weak."

"The labour market growth is not strong enough to push down the unemployment rate, and looking at the forward indicators we think it will push up in coming months," Peters said, adding the data reinforced why the RBA had lowered rates on Wednesday.

The impact of the three rate cuts delivered since July has yet to be seen on the labour market, but should help jobs growth by improving confidence and boosting activity through 1997, economists said.
However, the road to recovery will not be all clear sailing.
"The labour market still has a number of hurdles to clear," Colonial State Bank chief economist Hans Kunnen said.
"These include financial sector job rationalisations, the downsizing of the public sector, and job losses from Telstra," he said.
Others were more optimistic on the labour market outlook, although few were expecting signs of definite recovery to appear until the middle of 1997.

Citibank Australia chief economist Stephen Koukoulas said the figures were "pleasantly strong," and said that while it was too early to say that the worst had passed in the labour market, the unemployment rate may be consolidating between 8.5 and 8.75 percent, rather than moving towards the 9.0 percent level.
"The economy, and the labour market, are not in free fall and the raft of rate cuts over the past five months have set the scene for a stronger 1997," he said.
